lesson.menu_title: Hedging, Nuance and Discourse Markers -- Saying Where the Edge Is
lesson.menu_desc: The words you ADD to a claim so the room knows what is solid and what is an estimate: roughly, arguably, to be fair, having said that, it depends on -- and the diplomatic disagreement they make possible -- 31 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 17 -- Hedging, Nuance and Discourse Markers
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Lucia Nishiyama Serra | Lesson 17 -- Hedging, Nuance and Discourse Markers
phases: The Words That Mark the Edge

listenings.text: Two candidates, same question, and the difference is the reason I am writing this down. I asked both of them what the platform cost to run for a year. The first one gave me a number to the last dollar, with no pause at all. It was wrong by about forty percent, and we found that out ten minutes later. He never said he was not sure, so when the number failed, everything else he had told me failed with it. The second one said roughly two million, said it was the run rate and not the total, and offered to send the exact figure the same day. She was off by less than five percent, and even if she had been off by more, I would have believed the rest of her answer. That is the whole point. Hedging is not weakness here. A senior person marks which parts of the answer are solid and which parts are estimates, and that is what makes the solid parts worth something. The one thing I do not want is a wall of soft words with no claim underneath.

Here is something that surprises almost every executive I work with from outside the United States. In an American room, the careful sentence often sounds more senior than the confident one. That feels backwards, so let me explain why it happens. When you say roughly, or in my experience, or as far as I know, you are not apologizing. You are telling the room where the edge of your knowledge is. And a person who knows where that edge is has clearly been close to it. The person who never marks anything has either never been tested, or is hoping that nobody checks. Now, two warnings. First, one hedge per claim. If you stack them, if you say I think maybe it could possibly be around, the sentence stops carrying anything and the room stops listening. Second, the hedge has to be followed by something. Say roughly two million, and then commit to the exact figure. Say it depends on, and then name the condition. A hedge that leads nowhere is not nuance. It is just noise.

extra_audio.text: Tom asked me what the program cost to run for a year. I said roughly two million, and that it was the run rate and not the total. Off the top of my head I could not give him the exact figure, so I offered to send it the same day. Then he asked whether I agreed with the way his team evaluates models. To be fair, the coverage was strong. Having said that, I told him it was arguably still incomplete.
